body:
I plan to start on this one soon, one widget at a time to iterate on it. But here are the main points that I'm seeing:

## 1. Basic template and rendering

All our widgets should have sensible defaults in term of template and rendering so we understand how they work. This can be hiding unused links in pagination, or displaying our logo with the correct margin in the poweredBy or setting the currently selected facets in bold.

I see this part as embedded CSS using the weird `require('style?prepend!raw!./index.css');` syntax. All the elements we need to style will have a unique class (following the BEM model), so we can do a simple `.ais-{block}__{element}--{modifier}` selector in our CSS file to style them.

## 2. Adding custom classes to element

Users will want to override our styles with their own, or some they already have from popular libraries like Bootstrap. We should let them add a `form-control` class to an `input` if they want to.

For that, we will expose a `cssClasses` object on every object where user can define the CSS classes they want to add to the markup we generate.

## 3. Styling each element individually

For people that do not like big fat frameworks like Bootstrap that adds classes everywhere and would like more granularity on what is styled, we need a way to individually target any piece of markup we add. Fortunatly, we already kind of did that in **1**.

We'll just continue adding BEM classes to the markup we generate, even if we do not directly use it in the basic styling, this will in turn be usable by anyone. It means we'll have element with classes like `ais-pagination__link--disabled`, `ais-pagination__link-next`, `ais-pagination__wrapper`, etc.

## 4. Provide themes

Once we have all our elements that can easily be targeted with CSS, we can easily create themes, in the form of one `.css` file to be dropped in the page, to style all the widgets. We will use that to style instantsearch for a Magento or Shopify shop.
